value.overview: The Snowcap is a tiny, distinctive hummingbird of humid Central American forests. Adult males are famous for their brilliant white crown and deep coppery-purple plumage, which can appear nearly black in shade. Females are green above and pale below. This localized species frequents forest edges, openings, secondary growth, and flowering plantations, where it gathers nectar and small arthropods. It occurs from southern Honduras through Nicaragua and Costa Rica to western Panama.
value.classification: The Snowcap belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae in the order Apodiformes. Its scientific name is Microchera albocoronata, and two subspecies are generally recognized.
value.identification: The Snowcap measures about 6–7 cm long and has a short, nearly straight bill and a compact, short-tailed shape. The adult male is unmistakable, with an iridescent white crown, dark coppery-purple body, white undertail coverts, and some white in the tail. The female has metallic green upperparts, pale grayish-white underparts, and a patterned tail with white bases and tips separated by a broad dark band. Immature males initially resemble females and gradually acquire dark adult plumage.
value.rangeHabitat: The species has a localized Central American range extending from southern Honduras through Nicaragua and Costa Rica to western Panama. It occurs mainly on the Caribbean slope, with local populations on the Pacific slopes of Costa Rica and Panama. Snowcaps inhabit humid lowland and lower montane forest, especially edges, clearings, second growth, semi-open woodland, and shaded plantations. They are commonly associated with foothills and moderate elevations, although their exact elevation varies geographically and some birds move into lower country after breeding.
value.migrationStatus: A nonmigratory resident that makes local and seasonal elevational movements, often descending after breeding.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding occurs mainly from January through May; timing elsewhere is poorly documented. Males gather in loose leks, where they sing from perches, display to females, and chase rival males. The female alone builds a small cup nest from plant down, tree-fern scales, moss, and lichen, binding the materials with spider silk. It is usually attached to a slender twig or hanging vine about 1.7–3 m above the ground. The typical clutch contains two white eggs; incubation and fledging periods remain insufficiently documented.
value.dietFeeding: Snowcaps feed primarily on nectar from small flowers on trees, shrubs, vines, and epiphytes. They forage from the forest understory to the canopy and also visit flowering second growth and plantations. Their diet is supplemented with small arthropods, which may be gleaned from foliage or caught in short aerial sallies. Males sometimes defend productive flower patches against other Snowcaps but usually yield to larger hummingbirds.
value.behavior: This active hummingbird typically darts rapidly among shaded forest vegetation and flowering openings. Males defend feeding sites and participate in loose courtship leks, singing from exposed or partly concealed perches and pursuing rivals. Their calls include high, dry notes, buzzes, and chatters during aggressive encounters. Although often difficult to observe in dark vegetation, males may become conspicuous at favored flowers. Seasonal elevational movements appear to follow breeding conditions and changing nectar supplies.

conservation.status: Least Concern globally under the current IUCN assessment.
conservation.populationTrend: Decreasing; the global population has not been precisely quantified.
